question: Extending trailing-edge flaps generally affects stalling speed by:

options.text: Increasing the wing's maximum lift coefficient (CLmax), which lowers the stalling speed for a given weight
Decreasing CLmax, which raises the stalling speed
Having no effect, since flaps only change drag, not lift
Increasing the critical angle of attack to a higher value than the clean wing

explanation: Flaps increase the wing's effective camber, raising the maximum lift coefficient it can produce before stalling. Because stalling speed varies inversely with the square root of CLmax, a higher CLmax lets the wing support the aircraft's weight at a lower speed. Most flap types also somewhat reduce the critical angle of attack, not increase it.

question: Leading-edge slats improve high angle-of-attack performance primarily by:

options.text: Increasing wing area, which increases total lift at any angle of attack
Re-energising the boundary layer over the upper surface, delaying separation to a higher critical angle of attack
Reducing the wing's aspect ratio
Reducing induced drag at low speed

explanation: A slat opens a slot ahead of the leading edge that accelerates high-energy air from beneath the wing over the upper surface. This re-energised boundary layer resists separation for longer, letting the wing reach a higher angle of attack — and a higher CLmax — before stalling.

question: Compared with a plain (hinged) flap, a split flap, hinged only from the lower surface of the wing, tends to produce:

options.text: Less drag for the same lift increase
A similar or greater lift increase, but generally more drag, because the upper surface airflow separates behind the break in the surface
No change in CLmax at all
A higher critical Mach number

explanation: A split flap deflects only the lower surface, leaving the upper surface's contour broken at the hinge line. Airflow over the top tends to separate behind that break, giving a useful lift increase but at a higher drag cost than a plain flap of similar size — useful where a steep approach is wanted.

question: A slotted flap improves on a plain flap mainly by:

options.text: Increasing wing area only, with no aerodynamic slot effect
Opening a gap between the flap and the wing that channels high-energy air from below onto the flap's upper surface, re-energising its boundary layer and delaying separation
Reducing the flap's camber
Eliminating induced drag

explanation: The slot between the wing's trailing edge and the flap works the same way a leading-edge slot does: it lets higher-pressure air from below accelerate through the gap and re-energise the boundary layer over the flap's upper surface, allowing a larger flap deflection before that surface's airflow separates.

question: A Fowler flap differs from a simple slotted flap mainly because, as it extends, it:

options.text: Also moves aft, increasing wing area as well as camber
Rotates around a fixed hinge with no aft translation
Only deploys on the leading edge
Reduces wing area to increase speed

explanation: A Fowler flap rides aft on tracks as it extends, before rotating down — increasing both wing area and camber, on top of the slot effect a slotted flap already provides. This combination gives a particularly large increase in CLmax, which is why it is common on airliner wings.

question: A Krueger flap is a leading-edge high-lift device that, when deployed:

options.text: Hinges down and forward from the lower surface of the leading edge to increase camber ahead of the wing
Is a fixed leading-edge slot that never moves
Is a trailing-edge device only
Reduces the wing's angle of incidence

explanation: A Krueger flap folds out and down from underneath the leading edge, effectively extending and re-shaping it to add camber and delay separation at high angle of attack — a leading-edge alternative (or complement) to a slat, often used further inboard on a swept wing.

question: Compared with trailing-edge flaps, leading-edge devices such as slats primarily work by:

options.text: Increasing camber near the trailing edge
Raising the critical angle of attack itself, rather than mainly adding camber
Reducing wing area
Increasing induced drag only

explanation: Trailing-edge flaps mainly add camber, shifting the whole lift curve upward. Leading-edge devices instead mainly delay separation, extending the lift curve to a higher angle of attack before it stalls — two different mechanisms for raising CLmax, which is why aircraft often use both together.

question: Many transport aircraft wings use both leading-edge slats and trailing-edge flaps together mainly because:

options.text: Slats alone are always sufficient for any approach speed
The two devices raise CLmax through different, complementary mechanisms — a higher critical angle of attack from the slats and more camber from the flaps
Using both eliminates all drag during approach
They are required only for takeoff, never for landing

explanation: Because slats and flaps improve CLmax by different means — delaying the stall versus adding camber — combining them gives a larger total increase in maximum lift coefficient than either device could achieve alone, letting the aircraft fly a slower, safer approach and takeoff speed.

question: Extending flaps for approach increases drag as well as lift, which is operationally useful because it:

options.text: Reduces the power needed to fly a steeper approach path at a controllable, lower airspeed
Always increases the aircraft's range
Has no effect on approach speed
Is only relevant to jet aircraft

explanation: The extra drag from flaps lets a pilot fly a steeper, more controllable approach path at idle or near-idle power while still holding a safely low airspeed above the (also-reduced) stalling speed — rather than needing an unrealistically long, shallow, high-speed approach.

question: Many aircraft include a flap asymmetry protection system, whose purpose is to:

options.text: Increase the maximum flap extension speed
Detect and stop (or lock) flap movement if one side deploys differently from the other, preventing an uncontrollable rolling moment
Automatically retract the flaps at high speed only
Increase camber further on one wing intentionally

explanation: If flaps on one wing extended further than the other, the resulting difference in lift between the two wings could produce a rolling moment beyond the ailerons' authority to counter, especially at low speed. An asymmetry protection system halts or locks the flaps the moment such a difference is detected.

question: A triple-slotted flap, used on some older wide-body jet designs, achieves a very high CLmax mainly by:

options.text: Using three separate flap surfaces, each energised through its own slot, giving several stages of progressively increasing camber and slot-fed boundary layer control
Extending three times faster than a single-slotted flap
Eliminating induced drag entirely
Being a leading-edge device rather than a trailing-edge one

explanation: A triple-slotted flap comprises multiple flap elements deployed in sequence, each with its own slot re-energising the boundary layer over the next element downstream. This lets the whole assembly reach a very large usable deflection and camber increase without separating, at the cost of considerable mechanical complexity and weight.

question: The aft translation of a Fowler flap as it extends is typically achieved by:

options.text: A curved track and roller (or similar guided linkage) fixed to the wing structure, along which the flap rides aft before rotating down
A simple single hinge at the wing trailing edge, identical to a plain flap
Detaching the flap from the wing entirely during extension
Inflating the flap with compressed air

explanation: A Fowler flap's characteristic aft movement is produced by rollers or carriages running along a curved track fixed to the wing structure, guiding the flap aft (increasing wing area) before it rotates down to its final deflected position — a more mechanically complex arrangement than a simple hinged plain or slotted flap.

question: A "leading-edge flap" (such as a Krueger flap) differs from a "leading-edge slat" mainly in that:

options.text: A leading-edge flap mainly adds camber ahead of the wing without necessarily opening a slot, while a slat extends forward and down to open a slot that channels energising airflow onto the upper surface
The two terms describe exactly the same device with no difference
A leading-edge flap is always mounted at the trailing edge
A slat never affects the wing's angle of attack characteristics

explanation: Both raise CLmax and delay leading-edge separation, but a leading-edge flap (a hinged panel like a Krueger flap) mainly reshapes and adds camber to the leading edge, while a true slat's defining feature is the slot it opens, through which high-energy air is drawn over the upper surface to re-energise the boundary layer directly.

question: Extending trailing-edge flaps typically requires a trim change mainly because:

options.text: Flaps change the wing's camber and shift its center of pressure, altering the pitching moment about the center of gravity and requiring a compensating elevator/trim input
Flaps have no effect on pitching moment whatsoever
Flap extension always requires exactly the same trim change as gear extension
Trim changes are needed only when flaps are retracted, never when extended

explanation: Adding camber with flaps shifts the wing's center of pressure and changes the pitching moment it produces about the aircraft's center of gravity, so a compensating change in elevator deflection — and usually trim — is needed to hold the desired attitude, which is why a noticeable pitch change often accompanies flap selection.

question: The maximum flap extended speed, VFE, exists mainly because:

options.text: Flaps are structurally and aerodynamically designed for a limited speed range, and exceeding it risks structural damage to the flap or its mechanism
Flaps become more effective the faster the aircraft flies, with no upper limit
VFE only exists for aircraft with retractable landing gear
VFE is identical to the stalling speed for every aircraft

explanation: The extended flap surface and its actuating mechanism are designed to withstand the aerodynamic loads expected within a defined speed range. Beyond VFE, those loads can exceed what the flap structure or drive mechanism is built to handle, risking structural damage — hence the placarded limit.

question: Arriving over the runway threshold with excess airspeed while flaps are fully extended tends to produce a longer float during the flare mainly because:

options.text: The lower stalling speed and higher CLmax that flaps provide let the aircraft continue flying, just above the stall, for longer before it is slow enough to settle onto the runway
Flaps always shorten the flare regardless of approach speed
Flaps have no relationship to how long an aircraft floats
Excess speed has no effect on float distance

explanation: Because flaps lower the stalling speed, an aircraft arriving with excess airspeed can continue to fly, gradually decelerating in ground effect, for a longer distance before it slows enough to settle — floating further down the runway than an approach flown at the correct reference speed.

question: In a slotted flap's design, the "gap" and "overhang" refer to:

options.text: The width of the slot between the wing and flap, and how far the flap's leading edge sits ahead of the wing's trailing edge — both tuned to shape the energising jet of air through the slot
The total flap deflection angle and its maximum extension speed
The flap's total surface area and its weight
Terms that apply only to leading-edge slats, never to trailing-edge flaps

explanation: Gap (the slot's width) and overhang (how far forward the flap's leading edge sits relative to the wing's trailing edge) are both carefully tuned geometric parameters, since either being too large or too small can weaken the slot's boundary-layer-energising effect and reduce the flap's effectiveness.

question: Deploying roll spoilers on one wing while flaps are extended and the aircraft is close to its stalling speed requires particular care because:

options.text: The spoiler further reduces lift on that wing, on top of the already-reduced margin to the stall, and can bring that wing close to stalling ahead of the other
Spoilers always increase lift on the wing they are deployed on
Flaps and spoilers can never be used together on the same aircraft
Spoiler deployment has no effect on stall margin at any speed

explanation: A roll spoiler works by deliberately spoiling lift on one wing. Close to the stall, with margin already reduced by low speed, this can bring the spoiler-deployed wing uncomfortably close to (or past) its own local stalling angle of attack, which is why spoiler authority is often reduced or scheduled differently at low speed with flaps extended.

question: Leading-edge high-lift devices such as slats are frequently fitted with their own ice protection mainly because:

options.text: The leading edge is where ice accretes fastest, and ice on a slat or its track can both degrade the device's aerodynamic benefit and jam its extension mechanism
Ice never forms on leading-edge devices
Leading-edge devices are structurally immune to ice
Ice protection is only ever fitted to trailing-edge flaps

explanation: As the first surface the airflow (and any supercooled water droplets) meets, the leading edge accretes ice fastest of any part of the wing, and ice there both disrupts the aerodynamic performance a slat or leading-edge flap is meant to provide and risks jamming the mechanism that extends and retracts it — which is why these devices often carry dedicated anti-ice or de-ice protection.

question: A flap load relief system, fitted to some aircraft, is designed to:

options.text: Automatically reduce flap deflection (or limit further extension) if airspeed rises toward a level that would overstress the flap structure
Permanently lock the flaps in the fully extended position
Increase flap deflection automatically as airspeed increases
Only operate while the aircraft is on the ground

explanation: If airspeed inadvertently rises with flaps extended, a load relief system senses the increasing aerodynamic load and automatically reduces (or blocks further) flap deflection to keep loads within the structure's design limits, protecting the flap and its mechanism from an overspeed condition.

question: A double-slotted flap sits, in complexity and typical lift benefit, between:

options.text: A single-slotted flap and a triple-slotted flap, using two flap elements and two energising slots
A plain flap and a split flap only
A slat and a Krueger flap
A spoiler and a speed brake

explanation: A double-slotted flap uses two separate flap elements, each fed by its own slot, giving a larger CLmax increase and greater flexibility than a single-slotted flap while remaining mechanically simpler than a triple-slotted design — a common middle-ground choice on many airliner wings.

question: Some aircraft fit a seal or fairing over the flap well when the flaps are fully retracted, mainly to:

options.text: Reduce the parasite drag that an open, unsealed flap well would otherwise add in cruise
Increase flap deflection speed
Provide additional lift in cruise
Protect the flap only from ice

explanation: An open flap well or gap around a retracted flap can disturb the local airflow and add parasite drag even in cruise. A close-fitting seal or fairing keeps the wing's surface smooth when flaps are stowed, avoiding a drag penalty that would otherwise persist throughout the cruise phase of flight.

question: An "automatic" (as opposed to pilot-selected) leading-edge slat typically extends in response to:

options.text: Sensed angle of attack or airspeed approaching a threshold, extending on its own to raise the critical angle of attack when it is needed
A fixed schedule tied only to landing gear position
Cabin altitude
Engine oil temperature

explanation: Rather than being manually selected by the pilot, an automatic slat is driven out by aerodynamic loads or a dedicated sensor once angle of attack (or a corresponding low airspeed) approaches a set threshold, providing the stall-delaying benefit of a slat exactly when it is aerodynamically needed without requiring pilot action.

question: Flap asymmetry protection is often physically implemented using:

options.text: A mechanical torque-tube or cross-shaft connecting the flap drive on both wings, so an uneven load or jam on one side is detected and stops the whole system
Two entirely independent electrical systems with no mechanical or logical connection between the wings
A single flap panel shared by both wings
The autopilot alone, with no dedicated flap system involvement

explanation: Many flap systems drive both wings' flaps from a shared torque-tube or cross-shaft arrangement, so that a jam or excessive load difference on one side is mechanically detectable (through twist or a shear-pin failure, for instance) and halts flap movement before a large, uncommanded asymmetry can develop.

question: Compared with a purely mechanical slotted flap, a blown flap (using engine bleed air for boundary layer control) trades off:

options.text: A potentially higher CLmax against added complexity and the need to divert engine bleed air, which can reduce available thrust when the system is in use
Nothing at all — blown flaps are strictly superior in every respect with no downside
Being simpler and lighter than any mechanical slotted flap
Requiring no engine at all to function

explanation: A blown flap can push CLmax higher than a purely mechanical slot design, but it needs engine bleed air ducted to the flap, adding weight, complexity and maintenance, and diverting bleed air can measurably reduce the thrust or power otherwise available from the engine while the system is active.

question: A "circulation control wing", which blows a thin jet of air over a rounded trailing edge, increases lift by exploiting:

options.text: The Coandă effect, where the jet stays attached to the curved surface and deflects the surrounding flow, changing circulation around the wing without a conventional hinged flap
A conventional hinged flap identical to a plain flap
Increasing the wing's aspect ratio
Reducing engine power

explanation: Blown over a rounded (rather than sharp) trailing edge, the jet tends to follow the curved surface — the Coandă effect — pulling the surrounding flow around with it and changing the effective circulation, and hence lift, around the wing without needing a conventional moving flap surface at all.

question: Flaps are typically retracted in stages after takeoff, rather than all at once, mainly because:

options.text: Each stage of retraction raises stalling speed and reduces CLmax, so retraction is sequenced with acceleration to keep an adequate margin above the stall throughout
The flap motor is only able to move a small amount at a time
Staged retraction has no relationship to stalling speed
It is done purely to reduce noise

explanation: Because each stage of flap retraction reduces CLmax and raises stalling speed, retracting in scheduled stages as the aircraft accelerates keeps an adequate safety margin above the stall throughout the process, rather than risking an abrupt loss of lift margin if flaps were retracted all at once at too low a speed.

question: At the same flap deflection angle, a Fowler flap typically achieves a higher CLmax than a plain flap mainly because:

options.text: It adds usable wing area as it translates aft, on top of the camber increase a plain flap alone would provide
It always deflects through a larger angle than a plain flap
It eliminates induced drag
Plain and Fowler flaps always produce identical CLmax by design

explanation: Because a Fowler flap slides aft before rotating down, it increases the wing's effective area as well as its camber — an additional source of lift beyond what a plain flap's camber change alone provides at the same deflection angle, which is why Fowler flaps typically achieve a noticeably higher CLmax.

question: On a swept-wing airliner using both a Krueger flap and a slat, the Krueger flap is often found:

options.text: Inboard, where a pure camber-adding device is adequate, while the outboard wing — more prone to tip stall — carries the slat
Outboard only, with slats never used on the same wing
On the trailing edge, never the leading edge
Only on the vertical stabilizer

explanation: The outboard wing of a swept design is more prone to early tip stall and benefits most from a slat's slot-fed, angle-of-attack-raising effect, while the inboard wing — less prone to early separation — can often be adequately served by the simpler, purely camber-adding Krueger flap, which is a common reason the two devices appear together on the same wing.

question: An aircraft's landing reference speed, Vref, is generally defined with respect to high-lift devices as:

options.text: A fixed multiple (commonly around 1.3 times) of the stalling speed in the landing configuration, with landing flap extended
Exactly equal to the stalling speed in the landing configuration, with no margin
Unrelated to flap position
Always higher than the clean-configuration stalling speed

explanation: Vref is conventionally set at a fixed margin — commonly around 1.3 times — above the stalling speed in the full landing configuration, so the lower stalling speed that landing flap provides directly lowers the target approach speed, letting the aircraft fly a slower, shorter final approach with an adequate protective margin above the stall.
